dedupe_keys.name: replacing overhead lines with underground cables against storms and snow loads in finland elenia

description: This Climate-ADAPT case study follows Elenia, the second largest electricity distribution operator in Finland, in replacing overhead lines with underground cables. Storms, snow loads, lightning and tree fall cut overhead lines, and warmer climate is expected to keep deciduous trees in leaf longer and add deadwood. The 2013 update of the Electricity Market Act requires networks to be designed so that storms or snow loads cause blackouts of no more than 6 hours in towns and 36 hours elsewhere by 2028. Since 2009 Elenia has built only weather-proofed lines; cables are buried in trenches 0.45 to 1 m deep, often together with fibre-optic cable in co-construction with telecom companies, and GIS data tell excavators where cables lie. The underground share rose from 38 percent in 2016 to 41 percent in 2017, against a 75 percent target for 2028; 140 million euros were planned for 2018, and the national communication to the UNFCCC puts the needed distribution investment at 2,800 million euros. The page, published in 2018 and updated in 2026, is accessible online as free HTML. Coverage is Finland. Caveats: benefits are not yet quantified, and flood or landslide risk to cables is still hypothetical. It illustrates undergrounding as a storm resilience measure for outage and cost-benefit models of distribution grids. Related records: case_study-uk-overhead-line-ratings-rising-temperatures covers heat adaptation of lines.
